questions.question: What is the primary difference between scalability and elasticity?

options.text: Scalability is automatic, elasticity is manual
Scalability is planned growth, elasticity is automatic real-time adjustment
Scalability is for databases, elasticity is for web servers
There is no difference, they are the same concept

explanation.correct: Scalability involves planned capacity growth through manual resource additions, while elasticity automatically adjusts resources in real-time based on current demand metrics like CPU usage or request count.
explanation.why: Option A is backwards - elasticity is automatic. Option C incorrectly limits them to specific services. Option D is wrong as they are distinct concepts with different use cases and implementations.

questions.question: Which AWS service provides automatic elasticity for EC2 instances?

options.text: Amazon CloudWatch
AWS Auto Scaling
Elastic Load Balancer
Amazon VPC

explanation.correct: AWS Auto Scaling automatically launches or terminates EC2 instances based on defined policies and metrics, providing true elasticity by adjusting capacity in real-time.
explanation.why: CloudWatch monitors metrics but doesn't scale resources. Elastic Load Balancer distributes traffic but doesn't add/remove instances. VPC provides networking infrastructure, not scaling.

questions.question: What does vertical scaling involve?

options.text: Adding more servers to distribute workload
Upgrading CPU, RAM, or storage on a single server
Deploying across multiple Availability Zones
Using edge locations for content delivery

explanation.correct: Vertical scaling (scale-up/scale-down) means increasing or decreasing resources of a single instance, such as upgrading from t3.medium to t3.large for more CPU and RAM.
explanation.why: Option A describes horizontal scaling. Option C describes high availability architecture. Option D describes content delivery, not scaling.

questions.question: What is the main disadvantage of vertical scaling?

options.text: Requires application code changes
Cannot work with databases
Has physical hardware limits and creates single point of failure
Always costs more than horizontal scaling

explanation.correct: Vertical scaling is limited by maximum instance sizes available (physical ceiling) and creates a single point of failure since everything runs on one server. If that server fails, the entire application goes down.
explanation.why: Vertical scaling typically requires no code changes. It works well for databases. Cost comparison depends on workload - sometimes vertical is cheaper for small scales.

questions.question: How many Availability Zones does each AWS Region have at minimum?

options.text: 1 AZ
2 AZs
3 AZs
5 AZs

explanation.correct: Each AWS Region contains a minimum of 3 Availability Zones to ensure high availability and fault tolerance. Most Regions have 3-6 AZs.
explanation.why: 1 or 2 AZs wouldn't provide sufficient redundancy for enterprise workloads. While some Regions have more than 3 AZs, 3 is the minimum requirement.

questions.question: What is an AWS Region?

options.text: A single data center building
A geographic area with multiple isolated Availability Zones
A content delivery point for CloudFront
A virtual network in AWS

explanation.correct: An AWS Region is a geographic area (like US East, Europe, Asia Pacific) containing multiple isolated Availability Zones, each with one or more data centers. Regions are completely independent.
explanation.why: Option A describes a data center, not a Region. Option C describes an edge location. Option D describes a VPC.

questions.question: What happens to your EC2 instances when you switch AWS Regions in the console?

options.text: They automatically appear in the new Region
They disappear - resources are Region-specific
They migrate to the new Region
They become accessible from both Regions

explanation.correct: AWS Regions are completely isolated. Resources created in one Region only exist in that Region. When you switch to a different Region in the console, you won't see resources from other Regions.
explanation.why: Resources never automatically appear, migrate, or become accessible across Regions. You must explicitly configure cross-region replication or deployment if needed.

questions.question: What is the purpose of AWS edge locations?

options.text: Running EC2 instances closer to users
Caching content for faster delivery through CloudFront CDN
Providing backup data centers for Regions
Hosting databases for global access

explanation.correct: Edge locations are optimized for caching and delivering content (images, videos, files) to users with minimal latency through services like Amazon CloudFront CDN. They bring content physically closer to end users.
explanation.why: Edge locations don't run full EC2 instances, aren't backup facilities, and don't host traditional databases. They're specifically designed for content delivery and caching.

questions.question: Which of the following is a global AWS service?

options.text: Amazon EC2
Amazon RDS
Amazon CloudFront
Amazon VPC

explanation.correct: CloudFront is a global service that operates across all edge locations worldwide. When you configure it, it automatically distributes content globally without selecting a specific Region.
explanation.why: EC2, RDS, and VPC are all regional services - you must choose a specific Region when creating these resources.

questions.question: What is an Availability Zone?

options.text: A country or continent where AWS operates
One or more isolated data centers within a Region
A content caching location for CloudFront
A virtual server instance

explanation.correct: An Availability Zone (AZ) is one or more discrete data centers with redundant power, networking, and cooling within an AWS Region. Each AZ is physically separated but connected via high-speed links.
explanation.why: Option A describes a Region. Option C describes an edge location. Option D describes an EC2 instance.

questions.question: Your web application experiences traffic spikes every evening from 6 PM to 10 PM. Which approach best handles this?

options.text: Vertical scaling - upgrade to larger instance permanently
Horizontal scaling with Auto Scaling to add instances during spikes
Deploy to more Availability Zones
Use CloudFront edge locations

explanation.correct: Horizontal scaling with Auto Scaling Groups automatically launches additional instances during traffic spikes and terminates them when traffic drops, optimizing both performance and cost. This provides elasticity.
explanation.why: Vertical scaling keeps you paying for large instance 24/7 even when not needed. More AZs provide availability but don't add capacity. CloudFront helps with static content but doesn't add compute capacity.

questions.question: What is the typical latency between Availability Zones in the same Region?

options.text: 50-100 milliseconds
Sub-millisecond (less than 1ms)
5-10 seconds
100-200 milliseconds

explanation.correct: Availability Zones within the same Region are connected by high-speed, low-latency private network links providing sub-millisecond latency. This enables synchronous database replication and real-time coordination.
explanation.why: Higher latencies would prevent synchronous replication and coordinated operations. The private high-speed links between AZs ensure extremely low latency for intra-region communication.

questions.question: You need to comply with GDPR requiring European customer data stay in Europe. How do you configure this in AWS?

options.text: Use CloudFront to cache data in Europe
Deploy resources in an EU Region and configure services to not replicate elsewhere
Enable data encryption
Use VPC to isolate the data

explanation.correct: Deploy your application and store data in an EU Region (like eu-west-1 Ireland or eu-central-1 Frankfurt). AWS never moves data out of a Region unless you explicitly configure replication, ensuring compliance.
explanation.why: CloudFront caches globally by default. Encryption protects data but doesn't control location. VPC provides network isolation, not geographic data residency.

questions.question: Which statement about horizontal scaling is TRUE?

options.text: It requires stopping all servers to add new ones
It can only scale up, not down
It provides fault tolerance through redundancy across multiple instances
It's limited by maximum instance size

explanation.correct: Horizontal scaling distributes workload across multiple instances, providing fault tolerance - if one instance fails, others continue serving traffic. This redundancy is a key advantage over vertical scaling.
explanation.why: New instances can be added without stopping existing ones. Horizontal scaling works in both directions (scale-out and scale-in). Vertical scaling, not horizontal, is limited by instance size.

questions.question: Your database shows 95% CPU utilization constantly. What is the BEST immediate solution?

options.text: Add more database instances horizontally
Upgrade to a larger instance type (vertical scaling)
Deploy across more Availability Zones
Use CloudFront CDN

explanation.correct: For databases hitting CPU limits, vertical scaling (upgrading instance type for more CPU and RAM) is the quickest and most effective solution. Databases typically don't benefit from horizontal scaling for writes.
explanation.why: You can't horizontally scale a primary database for writes (read replicas help reads only). More AZs don't add CPU capacity. CloudFront doesn't reduce database CPU usage.

questions.question: What is the cost of data transfer between Availability Zones in the same Region?

options.text: Free - no charges
$0.01 per GB
$0.02 per GB
Same as internet data transfer rates

explanation.correct: Data transfer between AZs in the same Region is charged at $0.01 per GB in each direction. While not free, it's much cheaper than inter-region or internet transfer.
explanation.why: AZ-to-AZ transfer has a small cost to cover network infrastructure. It's not free, but significantly cheaper than cross-region transfer ($0.02/GB) or internet egress ($0.09/GB).

questions.question: How are Availability Zone names like 'us-east-1a' mapped to physical data centers?

options.text: All customers' us-east-1a maps to the same physical location
AZ names are randomized per account to distribute load evenly
They're mapped alphabetically by account creation date
They're assigned based on geographic proximity to customer

explanation.correct: AWS randomizes AZ name mappings per account. Your us-east-1a might be physically different from another customer's us-east-1a. This prevents all customers from concentrating resources in the same physical facilities.
explanation.why: If everyone's 'a' zones were identical, all customers would default to the same data center, creating hotspots. Randomization ensures even distribution across physical infrastructure.

questions.question: Which scenario is BEST suited for vertical scaling?

options.text: Stateless web application with variable traffic
Relational database requiring ACID transactions
Content delivery to global users
Microservices architecture

explanation.correct: Relational databases requiring ACID transactions benefit from vertical scaling because transactions must execute on a single server. Distributing transactional databases horizontally introduces complexity.
explanation.why: Stateless web apps should use horizontal scaling. Content delivery uses CloudFront/edge locations. Microservices are designed for horizontal scaling.

questions.question: What connects Availability Zones within a Region?

options.text: Public internet connections
Redundant, high-speed, low-latency private fiber links
Satellite connections
VPN tunnels

explanation.correct: AZs connect via redundant, dedicated fiber optic links providing high bandwidth (100+ Gbps) and sub-millisecond latency. This private network enables fast, secure communication between AZs.
explanation.why: Traffic between AZs never uses public internet for security and performance. Not satellite-based due to latency. More robust than VPN tunnels with dedicated infrastructure.

questions.question: You're launching a global video streaming service. Which AWS infrastructure should you prioritize?

options.text: Deploy only in the largest AWS Region
Use CloudFront edge locations with origin in one Region
Deploy in every AWS Region
Use Local Zones only

explanation.correct: CloudFront edge locations (400+ worldwide) cache and deliver video content from origins in one or more Regions. This provides global low-latency delivery without deploying full infrastructure in every Region.
explanation.why: Single Region without CDN creates latency for distant users. Deploying to all Regions is costly and complex for content delivery. Local Zones serve specific metros, not global distribution.

questions.question: Your application in us-east-1 needs to replicate data to eu-west-1 for disaster recovery. What is TRUE about this setup?

options.text: Data automatically replicates across Regions
You must explicitly configure cross-region replication and will incur data transfer costs
Replication is free between all AWS Regions
It's not possible to replicate between Regions

explanation.correct: Regions are isolated - you must explicitly configure cross-region replication using services like S3 Cross-Region Replication or database read replicas. Inter-region data transfer is charged at $0.02 per GB.
explanation.why: AWS never automatically replicates between Regions for data sovereignty. Cross-region transfer has costs. It's definitely possible but requires configuration.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of AWS Local Zones?

options.text: Lower pricing than standard Regions
Single-digit millisecond latency for users in specific metropolitan areas
Access to more AWS services than Regions
Better security than Availability Zones

explanation.correct: Local Zones extend AWS infrastructure into specific metro areas (like Los Angeles, Miami) to provide sub-10ms latency for users in those cities - ideal for gaming, streaming, and real-time applications.
explanation.why: Local Zones aren't cheaper, offer fewer services than full Regions, and have equivalent security. Their purpose is ultra-low latency for specific geographic areas.

questions.question: A startup plans to scale from 100 to 100,000 users over 2 years. Which architecture approach is BEST?

options.text: Start with vertical scaling, plan to refactor later
Design for horizontal scaling from day one with load balancers and stateless architecture
Wait until 10,000 users before implementing any scaling
Use only vertical scaling as it's simpler

explanation.correct: Design for horizontal scaling from the start - even with 2 servers behind a load balancer. This architecture scales linearly without requiring application refactoring. Re-architecting later is costly and risky.
explanation.why: Starting vertical and refactoring is expensive. Waiting until problems occur causes downtime. Pure vertical scaling hits limits and lacks redundancy at scale.

questions.question: What is AWS Wavelength designed for?

options.text: Faster internet speeds in AWS Regions
Ultra-low latency for 5G mobile applications by deploying at telecom network edges
Backup storage for critical data
Connecting on-premises data centers to AWS

explanation.correct: AWS Wavelength deploys AWS compute and storage at telecommunications providers' 5G network edge sites, enabling sub-5ms latency for mobile devices - critical for AR/VR, gaming, and IoT.
explanation.why: Not related to Region speeds or backup storage. Outposts, not Wavelength, connects on-premises to AWS. Wavelength specifically targets 5G edge computing.

questions.question: Your multi-tier application has stateful sessions. What must you implement for horizontal scaling?

options.text: Nothing - horizontal scaling works automatically
External session storage (like ElastiCache or DynamoDB) for session state
Larger instance types
More Availability Zones

explanation.correct: Stateful applications require external session storage so any server can handle any request. ElastiCache (Redis/Memcached) or DynamoDB centralize session data, enabling true stateless horizontal scaling.
explanation.why: Horizontal scaling requires stateless design - sessions stored locally break when load balancer routes to different server. Larger instances don't solve state management. AZs provide availability, not state management.

questions.question: What is the maximum latency AWS Wavelength Zones target?

options.text: Less than 100 milliseconds
Less than 50 milliseconds
Less than 10 milliseconds
Less than 5 milliseconds

explanation.correct: AWS Wavelength Zones target single-digit millisecond latency (typically under 5ms) by deploying compute resources directly at 5G cellular network sites, eliminating hops to distant data centers.
explanation.why: Standard Region latency is 50-200ms depending on distance. Local Zones target sub-10ms. Wavelength goes further, achieving sub-5ms for ultra-responsive mobile applications.

questions.question: Which combination provides the HIGHEST availability for a web application?

options.text: Single EC2 instance in one Availability Zone
Multiple EC2 instances in one Availability Zone
Multiple EC2 instances across multiple AZs with load balancer and Auto Scaling
Single large EC2 instance across multiple Regions

explanation.correct: Multi-AZ deployment with multiple instances, load balancer (distributes traffic and detects failures), and Auto Scaling (replaces failed instances) provides maximum availability. If one AZ fails, others continue.
explanation.why: Single instance has no redundancy. Single AZ creates regional point of failure. Single instance can't span Regions (instances are AZ-specific).

questions.question: Your application requires processing data within 1ms of generation on factory floor. Which AWS infrastructure is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Deploy in nearest AWS Region
Use Local Zones
Use AWS Outposts on-premises
Use CloudFront edge locations

explanation.correct: AWS Outposts brings AWS infrastructure to your on-premises data center, providing sub-millisecond latency for factory floor equipment. Network latency to any remote location (even Local Zones) exceeds 1ms.
explanation.why: Nearest Region likely 10-50ms away. Local Zones provide ~5-10ms. CloudFront is for content delivery, not compute. Only on-premises deployment meets sub-1ms requirement.

questions.question: What is the relationship between AWS Regions and data sovereignty?

options.text: AWS can move data between Regions for optimization
Data stays in the Region where you store it unless you configure cross-region replication
All data is automatically backed up globally
Regions share data for redundancy

explanation.correct: AWS guarantees data residency - data stored in a Region stays there unless you explicitly configure services like S3 Cross-Region Replication. This enables compliance with regulations like GDPR requiring data remain in specific countries.
explanation.why: AWS never automatically moves, shares, or backs up data across Regions. This regional isolation is fundamental to compliance and data sovereignty.

questions.question: For a truly globally distributed application with users worldwide, what architecture should you implement?

options.text: Deploy in one Region with CloudFront for content delivery
Deploy application tier in multiple Regions with Route 53 for DNS routing and CloudFront for content
Use only edge locations
Deploy in the largest Region only

explanation.correct: Multi-region deployment places application compute in regions close to user populations, Route 53 DNS routes users to nearest region, and CloudFront delivers static content globally. This provides lowest latency and highest availability.
explanation.why: Single Region creates latency for distant users. Edge locations don't run application logic. Largest Region doesn't mean closest to all users globally.
